newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr settles into range-trading routine.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr settles into range-trading routine.

text.p: The Australian dollar remained motionless through a desperatley quiet morning session in what dealers feared could easily become a pattern for the week.

There was some relief when rumours of a rate cut this morning proved wide of the mark, which allowed a modest bounce from a 75 cent low. The Reserve Bank's silence was taken as confirmation it would wait for its board meeting on July 1 before deciding on policy, but the market still had an easing priced in for the next month making it hard to sustain a rally.
A square market and a dearth of data added to expectations the US$0.7470/7540 range would hold true this week as well.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local dollar was dozing at US$0.7506/11 after an early US0.7503/08 and US$0.7511/16 late here Friday.

It had made it as high as US$0.7541 offshore Friday, its best level for the week, on U.S. and local bank buying but ran into sizeable sell orders before it could tackle important chart resistance at US$0.7550.
There was support at US$0.7490, US$0.7470 and US$0.7450 and a break of the latter would confirm a new phase of the three-month-old five-cent-wide downtrend with 73 cents as the main bear target.

The decline from 80 cents in March had largely been a function of disappearing interest rate differentials as an easing here and a hike in the U.S. brought official rates to par. And domestic money market rates had moved well below those in the U.S. as the market priced in another cut here and at least one more tightening in the U.S.

Those still bullish on the A$ longer term have long argued that commodity prices would come to its rescue. Above trend growth in the U.S. and recoveries in Japan and Europe, they argued, would lead to a synchronised pickup in world growth and so to higher demand for, and prices of, commodities.
Such a rise would be a boon for Australia where commodities like coal and copper make up over 60 percent of exports.
Many offshore investors also view the currency as a surrogate for commodity trends and it has shown a good correlation with prices in the past.

However, the recovery has been a long time in coming and often gains have been in sectors not much noted by offshore investors such as coal and wool. Base metals have improved led by copper, which recouped all the huge losses suffered in last year's Sumitomo scandal, and helped the RBA's index of commodity prices rise 3.6 points so far this year to 94.2.

However, many offshore funds tend to use the Commodity Research Bureau index of futures contracts which includes such un-Australian commodities as coffee, cocoa and orange juice while ommitting coal and wool the country's first and third biggest export earners respectively.
The CRB has been much more erratic this year, starting around 240.00 it rose to nearly 255.00 in late May only to tumble back to 240.52 by the end of last week.
Some of the recent volatility was due to wild swings in coffee prices, but the underlying performance of the index hardly suggested the price boom A$ bulls were hoping for.

Without a sustained pickup in commodity prices the dollar was likely to be dominated by interest differentials, and the outlook was not bright there with some analysts reckoning the U.S. will have to hike two or three times more to slow the economy sufficiently.
That process may start as soon as next week when the Federal Reserve holds its monthly policy meeting, although most analysts see an August move as more likely.
On the crosses the local dollar tracked a firmer US$/yen up to 86.75/85 yen from 85.90/00 late Friday and crept to 57.2 in trade weighted terms from 57.1. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
